question: How much did the standard salary level for the white-collar overtime exemptions change between the 2005 and 2020 editions of the regulations?
expected_answer: It rose from $455 per week in the 2005 edition to $684 per week in the 2020 edition.
expected_sources: 29 CFR Part 541 (2005 edition) | § 541.600; 29 CFR Part 541 (2020 edition) | § 541.600
notes: Checked against the cited sources. $455 (2005 edition) and $684 (2020 edition) confirmed.

question: The 2025 edition of the CFR lists $844 a week as the salary level for the overtime exemption. Is that the threshold that applies now?
expected_answer: No. Federal courts vacated the 2024 rule that set $844, and DOL's technical amendment effective May 15, 2026 (FR Doc. 2026-09839) restored the earlier text, so the current standard salary level is $684 per week.
expected_sources: 29 CFR Part 541 | § 541.600; FR Doc. 2026-09839 (Final rule, 2026-05-15) | Summary; 29 CFR Part 541 (2025 edition) | § 541.600
notes: Checked against the cited sources. Current § 541.600 says $684; FR Doc. 2026-09839 restores the pre-2024 text.

question: Can an employer deduct pay from an exempt employee's salary for hours of unpaid FMLA leave without losing the overtime exemption?
expected_answer: Yes. For unpaid FMLA leave the employer may pay a proportionate part of the salary for time actually worked (for example, deduct 10 percent for 4 hours of a 40-hour week) without affecting the exempt status.
notes: Checked against the cited sources. § 825.206(c) limits this to FMLA-eligible employees and FMLA-qualifying leave; the answer is fine without it.

question: What was the federal minimum wage once the 1977 amendments were fully phased in, and what did the 1989 amendments raise it to?
expected_answer: The 1977 amendments set $3.35 an hour after December 31, 1980; the 1989 amendments raised it to $3.80 on April 1, 1990 and $4.25 after March 31, 1991.
expected_sources: Pub. L. 95-151, Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1977 (91 Stat. 1245) | 91 Stat. 1245; Pub. L. 101-157, Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1989 (103 Stat. 938) | 103 Stat. 938
notes: Checked against the cited sources. $3.35 after Dec 31, 1980; $3.80 from Apr 1, 1990; $4.25 after Mar 31, 1991.

question: The 1977 FLSA amendments changed the monthly tip amount that makes someone a tipped employee. What was the change, and what is the threshold in the current regulations?
expected_answer: Effective January 1, 1978, the amount went from $20 to $30 a month; the current regulations still define a tipped employee as one who customarily and regularly receives more than $30 a month in tips.
expected_sources: Pub. L. 95-151, Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1977 (91 Stat. 1245) | 91 Stat. 1249; 29 CFR Part 531 | § 531.50
notes: Checked against the cited sources. $20 to $30 effective Jan 1, 1978; § 531.50(d) still says more than $30.

question: The 1985 FLSA amendments let public agencies give comp time instead of overtime pay. What accrual caps did they set, and does the current regulation keep them?
expected_answer: Up to 480 hours for public safety, emergency response or seasonal work and up to 240 hours for other work; § 553.21 keeps the same caps.
expected_sources: Pub. L. 99-150, Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1985 (99 Stat. 787) | 99 Stat. 788; 29 CFR Part 553 | § 553.21
notes: Checked against the cited sources. Tests that the system can say a rule has NOT changed.

question: Has the FMLA's 1,250-hour eligibility requirement changed since the law was passed in 1993?
expected_answer: No. The 1993 Act required at least 12 months with the employer and 1,250 hours of service in the previous 12 months, and § 825.110 still requires the same.
expected_sources: Pub. L. 103-3, Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (107 Stat. 6) | 107 Stat. 8; 29 CFR Part 825 | § 825.110
notes: Checked against the cited sources. Tests that the system can say a rule has NOT changed.

question: Under the 1997 rules, how much nonexempt work could an executive do and still be exempt, and how does the current rule treat it?
expected_answer: Under the 1997 long test, an executive could spend no more than 20 percent of weekly hours on nonexempt work (less than 40 percent in a retail or service establishment); the limit did not apply to an employee in sole charge of an independent or branch establishment or owning at least a 20 percent interest, nor to executives paid at least $250 a week under the short test. The current rule has no fixed percentage: exempt work must be the primary duty, and spending more than 50 percent of time on it is a useful guide but not the sole test.
notes: Checked against the cited sources. Fixed: the 1997 text says retail employees must not devote 'as much as 40 percent' (i.e. less than 40%), not 'no more than 40%'. Added the exceptions and the $250 short test, which had no percentage limit. Was: 'In 1997 an executive under the regular test could spend no more than 20 percent of hours (40 percent in a retail or service establishment) on nonexempt work. The current rule has no fixed percentage: ...'
